582.title: Bear one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2)
582.hook: and so you shall fulfill the law of Christ
582.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Stations of the Cross, especially in Lent, including the fifth station, where Simon of Cyrene helps Jesus carry the cross; the works of mercy put bearing burdens into practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karpos: one fruit of the Spirit with many flavors, grown rather than made. Your line was by their fruits.

Somebody in the congregation gets caught doing something wrong, and by Sunday everyone knows. You can feel the room choose sides. Paul knew that room. Near the end of Galatians he writes: if someone is overtaken in a fault, you who are spiritual should set him right in a spirit of gentleness, and keep an eye on yourself, in case you're tempted too. Then, in one short verse, he tells the whole church what to do with each other's weight.
screen: `CAUGHT, AND EVERYONE KNOWS.` → `SET HIM RIGHT, GENTLY.` → `WHAT TO DO WITH EACH OTHER'S WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ." The law of Christ. That's a striking phrase in this letter. Paul has spent five chapters arguing that Gentile believers don't need to take on the law of Moses. Now he names a law they do have to keep, and it's this one: carry each other. Christians connect it to Jesus's command at the Last Supper, to love one another as he has loved them. Then, three verses later, Paul seems to contradict himself: "For every one shall bear his own burden." Which is it? Carry each other's, or carry your own? Many readers find that the Greek helps. In the first verse the word is baros, a heavy, crushing weight, the kind no one should carry alone. In the second it's phortion, a pack, like the kit a soldier is expected to carry himself. So: share the crushing weights, and carry your own daily pack. Don't dump your pack on others, and don't leave anyone alone under a boulder. Catholics see this verse acted out at the fifth station of the cross, where Simon of Cyrene is made to help Jesus carry the cross. He didn't volunteer; the soldiers pressed him into it. Yet the Church remembers him for it, and many Catholics pray before that station every Lent. The works of mercy put the verse into daily practice too: comfort the sorrowful, visit the sick, bear wrongs patiently. Notice that Paul doesn't say to fix each other's burdens. Often you can't. You can only take a corner of the weight.
screen: `THE LAW OF CHRIST: CARRY EACH OTHER.` · `BAROS: THE CRUSHING WEIGHT.` · `PHORTION: YOUR OWN PACK.` · `SIMON OF CYRENE: THE FIFTH STATION.` · then, large: `BEAR YE ONE ANOTHER'S BURDENS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone carrying something too heavy right now: an illness, a debt, a child in trouble, grief. Don't try to solve it; just ask what one corner you could lift, a meal, a ride, an hour of sitting with them, a call where you mostly listen. If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, hold them in mind with that one thing.
Baros. The crushing weight Paul says we should share for each other, not the daily pack everyone carries alone. Today's word.
Your line: bear one another. Share the boulders, and carry your own pack. That's day five hundred eighty-two.

583.title: By grace, not of yourselves (Ephesians 2:8–10)
583.hook: saved by grace through faith, created for good works
583.howItsDone: Catholics teach that justification is a free gift of grace that no one can merit, and that grace also makes good works possible; in 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint declaration on justification.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baros and phortion: share the crushing weights, carry your own pack. Your line was bear one another.

On October thirty-first, 1999, in the German city of Augsburg, representatives of the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint declaration. It was about a question that had divided them since the sixteenth century: how is a person made right with God? Today's verses sat near the center of that long argument. They come from Ephesians, the first of a new stretch of letters. Tradition says Paul wrote them as a prisoner, in chains.
screen: `AUGSBURG, OCTOBER 1999.` → `AN ARGUMENT FROM THE 1500S.` → `LETTERS FROM PRISON.`

segments.voice: Ephesians chapter two starts with a hard picture: you were dead in your sins. Then the turn: God, who is rich in mercy, brought us to life with Christ. Then the verses: "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God; Not of works, that no man may glory." A gift. Not wages. Nobody can take credit for it. But Paul doesn't stop there, and readers who stop at verse nine miss the next line: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus in good works, which God hath prepared that we should walk in them." Saved by grace, and made for good works. Not saved by good works, and not saved from doing them. The works were prepared in advance, like a path laid down for you to walk on. The Greek word for workmanship is poiēma: something made, a crafted thing. Here it means God's handiwork. Catholics and Protestants argued for centuries over how grace, faith and works fit together. The Catholic Church taught at the Council of Trent that nothing before justification, neither faith nor works, earns the grace of justification. And in the 1999 declaration, Catholics and Lutherans said together that by grace alone, in faith in Christ, and not because of any merit, we are accepted by God and receive the Holy Spirit, who renews our hearts and calls us to good works. Some differences remain, and both sides say so. But on this, they found they could speak with one voice.
screen: `DEAD, THEN MADE ALIVE.` · `A GIFT, NOT WAGES.` · `HIS WORKMANSHIP: POIĒMA.` · `CATHOLICS AND LUTHERANS, 1999.` · then, large: `BY GRACE YOU ARE SAVED THROUGH FAITH.`

segments.voice: Turn your hands palm up on your knees and think of one good thing you didn't earn: a person, your health, a morning, your faith if you have it. Then turn your hands over, ready to work, and think of one good thing that seems to be waiting for you to do. If you pray, give thanks, then ask for help to do it; if not, simply receive, then decide.
By grace. Paul's words to the Ephesians: saved by God's gift, not by works, and then made for the good works God prepared. Today's word.
Your line: his workmanship. A gift first, then a path to walk. See you tomorrow.

584.title: Breadth, length, height, depth (Ephesians 3:14–19)
584.hook: Paul kneels and prays they know the love that surpasses knowledge
584.tomorrow: One Lord, one faith, one baptism
584.howItsDone: Catholics kneel during parts of the Mass, including the consecration in the Eucharistic Prayer, before the Blessed Sacrament, and often at private prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, by grace: a gift, not wages, and then good works to walk in. Your line was his workmanship.

The Council of Nicaea, in 325, asked Christians to stand for prayer on Sundays and through the days of Pentecost. In scripture, kneeling comes with a plea more than once: Solomon kneels to dedicate the temple, and Jesus kneels in the garden. So when Paul writes, in the middle of Ephesians, for this cause I bow my knees, the posture carries weight. He's on the floor. And what he asks for, down there, is not for himself.
screen: `NICAEA: STAND TO PRAY ON SUNDAYS.` → `SOLOMON AND JESUS KNEEL.` → `I BOW MY KNEES.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "For this cause I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." He prays that they'll be strengthened in the inner man, that Christ may dwell in their hearts by faith, and then: "that being rooted and founded in charity, you may be able to comprehend, with all the saints, what is the breadth, and length, and height, and depth." Two pictures in one phrase. Rooted, like a tree. Founded, like a building. Love underground, holding everything up. And then four dimensions. Breadth, length, height, depth of what? Paul doesn't say. He leaves the sentence open, as if the thing were too large to name. Readers have filled the space for centuries. Saint Augustine saw the shape of the cross: the breadth of the crossbeam where the arms were stretched, the length of the upright, the height reaching up, the depth sunk in the ground. Others hear simply the size of God's love in every direction. Then Paul says what it all points to: "To know also the charity of Christ, which surpasseth all knowledge." To know what can't be known. It's a deliberate paradox. In Paul's picture, this love can't be measured, and yet he prays they will come to know it, the way you know someone you love without being able to explain them. Catholics still kneel at weighty moments: at the consecration during Mass, before the tabernacle, in confession. The posture says what Paul's says. This is too big to meet standing up.
screen: `I BOW MY KNEES.` · `ROOTED AND FOUNDED: A TREE, A HOUSE.` · `FOUR DIMENSIONS, AND NO NOUN.` · `TO KNOW WHAT SURPASSES KNOWLEDGE.` · then, large: `THE BREADTH, AND LENGTH, AND HEIGHT, AND DEPTH.`

segments.voice: If your body allows, kneel on the floor or a cushion; if not, sit and bow your head low, and feel how different it is from standing: lower, smaller, steadier. Picture something stretching out from you, wide, long, high and deep, without naming it yet. If you pray, pray for someone else, the way Paul did on his knees; if not, stay low and still, and let the room be large around you.
Breadth. The first of Paul's four dimensions: breadth, length, height and depth, the size of a love that surpasses knowledge. Today's word.
Your line: rooted in charity. Roots underneath, and love in every direction. Day five hundred eighty-four, in the books.

585.title: One Lord, one faith, one baptism (Ephesians 4:1–6)
585.hook: keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace
585.howItsDone: Catholics profess "one baptism for the forgiveness of sins" in the Creed at Sunday Mass, and the Church recognizes the baptism of other Christians baptized with water in the name of the Trinity, so it is not repeated.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul on his knees, praying for the breadth, length, height and depth. Your line was rooted in charity.

Some families have a quarrel that comes back every holiday: the same two people, the same old topic, the same tight silence over dessert. Churches have them too, and the church Paul writes to in Ephesians was mixed: Jews and Gentiles, people who'd grown up with very different ways. So he opens the second half of the letter by begging them, as a prisoner in the Lord, to walk worthy of their calling: with humility, gentleness and patience, bearing with one another in love. And then he tells them what they're keeping.
screen: `THE QUARREL THAT COMES BACK.` → `A CHURCH OF JEWS AND GENTILES.` → `A PRISONER BEGS THEM.`

segments.voice: "Careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." Notice the verb. Keep, not make. Paul doesn't tell them to build unity from scratch. He says it's already given, and their job is to guard it. The word for bond is syndesmos, the same word a verse in Colossians uses for the ligaments that hold a body together. Peace is the ligament. Then he counts: "One body and one Spirit; as you are called in one hope of your calling. One Lord, one faith, one baptism. One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in us all." Count the ones. Body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, God. Seven. It sounds like something sung or recited, and scholars think Paul may be echoing words the churches already used. Catholics recite a descendant of that list every Sunday in the Creed: one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church, and one baptism for the forgiveness of sins. And that one baptism matters for how Catholics see other Christians. The Second Vatican Council taught that baptism is a sacramental bond of unity among all who are reborn by it. When a baptized Protestant Christian becomes Catholic, the Church does not baptize them again, as long as the baptism was with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. One baptism. The Church says plainly that full unity is not yet here. But Paul's verb still stands: keep. Something is already shared, and it can be guarded or neglected.

segments.voice: Think of one quarrel in your life, small or old, and picture the other person, not the argument. Notice something you still share, a family, a street, a history, maybe a faith, and one small step that would keep the peace instead of winning. If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, simply wish them well, and mean it.
One Lord. From Paul's seven ones in Ephesians: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all. Today's word.
Your line: keep the bond of peace. It's already given; it only needs keeping. Until tomorrow.

586.title: The armor of God (Ephesians 6:10–17)
586.hook: truth as a belt, faith as a shield, the word as a sword
586.howItsDone: Some Catholics pray a morning offering as they begin the day, and some pray Saint Patrick's Breastplate, a prayer traditionally attributed to Patrick that asks Christ's protection on every side.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seven ones: one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and a peace to keep. Your line was keep the bond of peace.

Someone chained to a Roman soldier for months would come to know his kit by heart. The belt. The breastplate. The sandals. The tall shield, the helmet, the short sword. Acts says that in Rome Paul lived under guard with a soldier, and in Ephesians he calls himself an ambassador in a chain. Whether or not he wrote this looking at a guard, the picture he paints at the end of the letter is unmistakable. He dresses the whole church for battle.
screen: `CHAINED TO A SOLDIER.` → `BELT, BREASTPLATE, SHIELD, SWORD.` → `A CHURCH DRESSED FOR BATTLE.`

segments.voice: "Put you on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the deceits of the devil." The word for the full armor is panoplia: every piece, head to foot. Then Paul says who the enemy is: our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers and the spirits of wickedness. Not people. In Paul's picture, the enemy is never the person across the table. Then he hands out the kit, piece by piece. Truth as a belt, holding everything in place. The breastplate of justice; the Douay-Rheims says justice, following the Latin, where the King James says righteousness. Feet ready with the gospel of peace. Then "the shield of faith," to quench the fiery darts of the most wicked one. The helmet of salvation. And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. Look at the list again. Almost everything in it is for standing, not attacking. Paul's verb is stand, over and over. The only weapon is the sword, and it's made of words: God's word. Much of this comes from the prophet Isaiah, where God himself puts on justice as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation. So the armor is God's own, lent out. The armor picture lives on in prayer. An old Irish prayer called Saint Patrick's Breastplate, attributed by tradition to Patrick, asks Christ to surround the one praying on every side, and some people pray it as they start the day.

segments.voice: Touch your head, helmet; your chest, breastplate; your waist, belt; your feet, shoes; and with each, think one word: hope, justice, truth, peace. Then name one thing you'll need to stand firm against today, a temptation, a lie, a fear, but not a person. If you pray, pray through Paul's list; if not, let the four touches remind you what you want to carry.
Panoplia. Full armor, every piece, head to foot: Paul's picture of the Christian dressed in truth, justice, peace, faith and the word of God. Today's word.
Your line: put on the armor. Almost all of it is for standing. Day five hundred eighty-six, done.

587.title: He emptied himself (Philippians 2:5–11)
587.hook: the early hymn of Christ taking the form of a servant
587.howItsDone: Catholics hear the hymn of Philippians 2 as the second reading on Palm Sunday, and the liturgy calls for a bow of the head at the name of Jesus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, panoplia: the full armor of God, almost all of it for standing firm. Your line was put on the armor.

Around the year 112, a Roman governor named Pliny wrote to the emperor Trajan about the Christians in his province. He'd questioned some of them. They met on a fixed day before dawn, he reported, and sang a hymn to Christ as to a god. We don't have their words. But many scholars think one of the earliest Christian hymns sits in today's passage, older than the letter it's in, quoted by Paul to his friends in Philippi.
screen: `A GOVERNOR'S LETTER, AROUND 112.` → `A HYMN TO CHRIST BEFORE DAWN.` → `ONE OF THE EARLIEST HYMNS.`

segments.voice: Paul sets it up with a request: in humility, count others better than yourselves. "For let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus." Then the hymn: "Who being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and in habit found as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even to the death of the cross." Emptied himself. The Greek verb is ekenōsen, and from it comes today's word: kenosis, self-emptying. Emptied of what? Paul doesn't spell it out. Catholic teaching, following the Council of Chalcedon, holds that he did not stop being God. He emptied himself by taking on what he was not: a human nature, a servant's form, a death reserved for slaves and rebels. The hymn goes down: God, servant, man, death, the cross. Then it turns and goes up: God exalted him and gave him the name above every name, "That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth." Down to the lowest point, then raised to the highest. Paul isn't writing a doctrine lesson. He's asking a quarrelsome church to have the same mind: go down first. Catholics hear this hymn every year on Palm Sunday, at the start of Holy Week. And at Mass, the liturgy's instructions still call for a bow of the head at the name of Jesus.
screen: `LET THIS MIND BE IN YOU.` · `KENOSIS: HE EMPTIED HIMSELF.` · `STILL GOD, TAKING A SERVANT'S FORM.` · `DOWN TO THE CROSS, THEN RAISED UP.` · then, large: `EVERY KNEE SHOULD BOW.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you hold onto that keeps you above other people: the need to be right, to get credit, to be served first. Picture taking it out of your pocket and setting it on the table, and notice how it feels to be without it, even for a minute. If you pray, say the name of Jesus slowly and bow your head; if not, simply bow your head, and let it stay on the table.
Kenosis. Greek for self-emptying, from Philippians: Christ, in the form of God, emptied himself and took the form of a servant. Today's word.
Your line: obedient unto death. Down to the lowest point, then raised up. See you tomorrow.

empty yourself, taking the form of a servant.

original.note: Greek: emptying, from the verb ekenōsen, 'he emptied' (Philippians 2:7).

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about humility.
what it means: Christ came down from the form of God to a servant's death, and God raised him above every name.
what a scholar hears: an early Christ-hymn, likely older than the letter; ekenōsen; a V-shaped descent and ascent.

a fast that empties the body before prayer

chat.says: Why would Paul quote a hymn about Christ emptying himself to a quarreling church?
options: So they'd have the same mind: go down first, as Christ took a servant's form.
To settle an argument in Philippi about the right date for Easter.
To prove to his rivals that he had written the hymn himself.
chat.meaning: Paul asks a quarrelsome church: let this mind be in you. Christ went down to a servant's death, then was raised up.

588.title: Forgetting what's behind (Philippians 3:13–14)
588.howItsDone: Catholics confess their sins in the sacrament of penance and believe absolved sins are truly forgiven; confessors counsel people troubled by scruples not to re-confess sins already forgiven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kenosis: he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Your line was obedient unto death.

Paul had two pasts, and either one could have held him in place. The first was a past to be proud of. In Philippians he lists it: circumcised on the eighth day, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, blameless in keeping the law. The second was a past to be haunted by. He'd persecuted the church, dragging believers off to prison. One past could make him proud. The other could make him despair. Today he says what he does with both.
screen: `A PAST TO BE PROUD OF.` → `A PAST TO BE HAUNTED BY.` → `WHAT HE DOES WITH BOTH.`

segments.voice: He's just said he counts all his gains as loss for the sake of knowing Christ. Then: "Brethren, I do not count myself to have apprehended. But one thing I do: forgetting the things that are behind, and stretching forth myself to those that are before, I press towards the mark, to the prize of the supernal vocation of God in Christ Jesus." It's a runner's sentence. Stretching forth is one Greek word, epekteinomenos, straining forward, like a runner leaning toward the finish. The mark is the finish post a runner fixes his eyes on. The prize is the wreath at the end. Supernal vocation means the upward call: God calling from above. Now notice what forgetting can't mean here. Paul hasn't lost his memory. He's just listed his whole past in detail. Forgetting means the past no longer steers. A runner knows the track behind him is there. He just doesn't run looking at it. And Paul says plainly he hasn't arrived. He's still running. Saint Gregory of Nyssa built a whole picture of the spiritual life on this one word. He said the soul never stops stretching toward God, because God never runs out. Catholics put this into practice in confession. The Church teaches that sins confessed and absolved are truly forgiven, and a confessor may tell someone who keeps re-confessing old sins, out of worry, to stop: it's already behind you. The pride and the shame both get left on the track. One thing I do, Paul says. Just one.
screen: `I HAVE NOT ARRIVED.` · `A RUNNER STRAINING FORWARD.` · `FORGETTING: THE PAST NO LONGER STEERS.` · `ALWAYS STRETCHING TOWARD GOD.` · then, large: `I PRESS TOWARDS THE MARK.`

segments.voice: Think of one old failure you still replay: something you said, a year you wasted, a way you hurt someone. If you've made it right, confessed it, or done what you could, picture it on the track behind you, then turn and face forward, toward one step today. If you pray, hand the old failure to God and ask for the next step; if not, simply notice which way you're facing.
Forgetting what's behind. Paul's runner's sentence: forgetting the past, stretching toward what's ahead, pressing toward the mark. Today's word.
Your line: press on. And that's week eighty-four: baros, by grace, breadth, one Lord, panoplia, kenosis, and forgetting what's behind. That's day five hundred eighty-eight.
screen: `WEEK EIGHTY-FOUR: BURDENS · GRACE · BREADTH · ONE LORD · ARMOR · KENOSIS · FORWARD`

fork.setup: you're Paul, with a proud record and a shameful one. what do you do with them?
options: build on the proud one and hide the other.
keep confessing the shameful one forever.
forget what's behind and press towards the mark.
fork.reveal: "forgetting the things that are behind, and stretching forth myself to those that are before, I press towards the mark."

original.note: Greek: a mark to aim at, the goal a runner fixes his eyes on (Philippians 3:14).

trapdoor: what you thought: try not to think about the past.
what it means: neither pride nor shame from the past steers you; you run toward God's upward call.
what a scholar hears: epekteinomenos, the runner's lean, which Gregory of Nyssa made into epektasis, the soul's endless stretching into God.
guess: letting the past stop steering while you run on
wiping every memory of your past for good
pretending your old mistakes never happened

chat.says: How can Paul say he forgets what's behind, right after listing his whole past?
options: Forgetting means the past no longer steers him, like a runner who doesn't look back.
He meant only his sins; his good record he was meant to keep remembering.
He wrote that line years earlier, before he ever listed his past.
chat.meaning: Paul hasn't lost his memory. Forgetting means the past, proud or shameful, no longer steers; he strains forward like a runner.
